hints: Collapse each strongly connected component (SCC); the components of a tournament form a directed acyclic graph.
Between any two SCCs all edges point the same way, so the condensation is a transitive tournament and has a unique order.
Count by the first SCC: choose its vertices and a strongly connected tournament on them, then count the remaining components.
analogy: A tournament breaks into an ordered sequence of strongly connected blocks, with every edge between blocks pointing forward.
example: For n=3 there are 8 tournaments: 2 directed 3-cycles have one SCC, 6 transitive tournaments have three SCCs, and none have exactly two SCCs. The output is 2, 0, 6.
algorithm: Let F[n]=2^(n choose 2), the number of all tournaments, and g[n] the number that are strongly connected. Set g[1]=1 and compute g[n]=F[n]-?(s=1..n-1) C(n,s)g[s]F[n-s] modulo MOD by considering the first SCC. Set dp[0][0]=1. For each n?1 and k?1 compute dp[n][k]=?(s=1..n) C(n,s)g[s]dp[n-s][k-1]. Print dp[n][k] for k=1..n. Precompute binomial coefficients and powers of two modulo MOD.
correctness: The SCC condensation of a tournament is itself a tournament and is acyclic; an acyclic tournament has a unique total order, with all cross-component edges directed forward. Thus every tournament decomposes uniquely into an ordered sequence of strongly connected blocks. The recurrence for g subtracts all decompositions whose first block is smaller than n from the total F[n]. The dp recurrence chooses the first block?s labels and strongly connected internal tournament, then uniquely counts the remaining ordered blocks. Hence dp[n][k] counts exactly tournaments with k SCCs.
complexity: O(n?) time and O(n?) space for the recurrences and binomial coefficients, where n?500.
